segments.text: A payment service container ran out of memory every 3 hours. The culprit? A
startup handler that opened AO sessions, but shutdown never closed them because
an exception skipped registration. Let's break down FastAPI lifespan
events, startup, shutdown, and context managers, how it works, and the exact
mistake behind that failure. Think of your FastAPI app as a food
truck. Startup is when you open the shutters, turn on the grill, and stock
the fridge. Shutdown is when you clean up, turn off the gas, and lock up. The
lifespan context manager is like a checklist that guarantees you do both in
order, even if a health inspector shows up mid-shift.
The old decorators look clean, but hide a nasty flaw. They don't compose. If you
have three startup handlers, and the second one throws, the first one's
resources never get cleaned up. In production, that means leaked
connections, open file handles, and zombie threads.
Here's the bug in action. If the second startup handler raises an exception, the
shutdown handler never runs, and the database pool is leaked. This is exactly
what caused the OOM incident. FastAPI's lifespan parameter accepts an
async generator. Everything before yield is startup. Everything after is
shutdown. The generator is wrapped in a context manager, so even if startup
throws, the cleanup runs. This is the only pattern you should use in
production. Here's how a checkout service
initializes its database pool, cache client, and external payment gateway
client. Notice the try finally belt and suspenders. Even though the context
manager already guarantees cleanup, it makes the intent explicit.
When Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, your app has a few seconds to finish
in-flight requests and close resources. The lifespan shutdown runs after the
server stops accepting new connections, but before the process exits.
Always wrap cleanup in a anycio wait with a timeout.
Here's the pattern for graceful shutdown. We cancel all background tasks
and then wait for them to finish with a timeout. Never use anycio gather without
a timeout in shutdown. It can hang forever.
You can't test lifespan events with a simple test client because it doesn't
trigger the lifespan by default. You need to manually enter the lifespan
context using app router lifespan context. This catches the exact bug that
burned us in the incident. Here's how we test the checkout service
lifespan. We assert that the pool is created after startup and closed after
shutdown. Knowing that test client doesn't trigger
lifespan by default is a common interview trap.
If you're writing a tiny internal tool that runs one request and exits, don't
bother with lifespan. Just open connections in the endpoint and close
them in a finally. But for any service that stays running and handles
concurrent requests, lifespan is non-negotiable.
For a cron job style script that calls one API and dies, a simple with block is
cleaner. But the moment you add a second route
that uses the same database, refactor to lifespan before you forget.
Sometimes you need to pass lifespan resources to background tasks or
dependencies. The cleanest pattern is to store them in
app state and access them via request app state and dependencies. But beware.
Background tasks that outlive the request may try to access app state
after shutdown. Here's the pattern for dependency
injection with lifespan. The get DB dependency accesses the pool
from app state. Never store resources in global variables. Use app state, it's
designed for this and works with multiple workers.
This is the same we highlighted at the start. Here's exactly why that happened.
The old at app on event decorator opened a new A up session on every worker
start, but when another startup handler crashed, the shutdown never ran.
Sessions accumulated until the container ran out of memory every 3 hours.
The old at app on event decorators do not compose. If one startup handler
crashes, previous handlers resources are never cleaned up, leading to connection
leaks and OOM. The fix was to replace both decorators
with a single lifespan context manager. The yield cleanup runs even if startup
partially fails. We added session close in a finally block. This ensures the
session is always closed, preventing the leak.
This is the exact mistake from the incident. The startup handler opens a
session, but if another startup handler crashes, the shutdown never runs and the
session leaks. Always use the lifespan context manager
to pair startup and shutdown. Never store resources in global
variables. Use app state. It's designed for this and works with multiple
workers. Global variables can cause race
conditions and are not safe in multi-process deployments.
Never use asyncio.gather without a timeout in shutdown. If one task hangs,
your entire shutdown hangs and Uvicorn kills the process ungracefully. Always
use asyncio.wait with a timeout. The lifespan parameter was introduced in
FastAPI March 2023. If you are on an older
version, you must upgrade or continue using the deprecated at app on event
decorators. Check your FastAPI version with fast api
version or import FastAPI.print FastAPI.version.
To ensure your app shuts down within a specific time, configure timeout
graceful shutdown in Uvicorn. This complements the asyncio wait timeout in
your lifespan shutdown. Example, run with Uvicorn app app timeout graceful
shutdown 10 to allow at most 10 seconds for shutdown.
When running with multiple workers, e.g. Uvicorn workers four, each worker runs
its own lifespan independently. Resources like database connection pools
are per process. Do not assume shared memory between workers. Use external
services, Redis, PostgreSQL for cross-worker state. Lifespan ensures
each worker cleans up its own resources. Here's how to diagnose and fix the
common failure modes. First, check if you're using the deprecated at app on
event. Replace it with the lifespan context manager. Ensure pool close is
called in a finally block. For shutdown hangs, use asyncio wait with a timeout.
Let's run through some common interview questions. How does lifespan handle
exceptions during startup? Context managers exit runs cleanup after yield,
releasing acquired resources. When to use lifespan vs. with block? Lifespan
for long-running services with shared state, with block for single endpoint
scripts. What happens if you forget to cancel
background tasks in shutdown? Tasks prevent event loop from closing. Uvicorn
kills process after timeout. And a few frequently asked questions.
